blocks.title: The light microscope
blocks.md: A **microscope** lets us see things that are too small for the eye. Light passes through a thin specimen on the **stage**. The **objective lens** makes a first image and the **eyepiece lens** makes it bigger. A **mirror or lamp** gives light. The **focusing knobs** move the lens to make the image sharp.

blocks.caption: A light microscope (schematic).
blocks.alt: A simple drawing of a microscope with eyepiece lens, body tube, objective lens, stage, mirror or lamp and focusing knob labelled.

blocks.title: Total magnification
blocks.md:
**Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.**

Example: eyepiece ×10 and objective ×40 gives ×400.

Start with the **lowest power** objective; find the specimen; then change to a stronger lens and use the fine focus only.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Never use the coarse focus with a high-power lens: you can break the slide.
- A specimen must be **thin** so that light passes through it.
- Do not add the two magnifications; **multiply** them.

blocks.title: Total magnification
blocks.statement: A student uses an eyepiece lens of ×10 and an objective lens of ×40. Find the total magnification.

blocks.title: Which lens first?
blocks.statement: You have objectives of ×4, ×10 and ×40. Which should you use first, and why?
steps: The ×4 lens has the widest field of view and is furthest from the slide.
It is easiest to find the specimen with it, then switch to a stronger lens.

lessons.title: Plant and animal cells
lessons.programRef: Form 4 Biology — Cells, microscope, tissues (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)

objectives: Name the parts of a cell and give their jobs.
List the differences between plant and animal cells.
Explain what tissues, organs and systems are.
reviewNotes: Level: introductory; check whether Form 4 syllabus includes cell specialisation examples.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Parts of a cell
blocks.md:
- **Cell membrane**: controls what goes in and out.
- **Cytoplasm**: where chemical reactions happen.
- **Nucleus**: controls the cell and holds the genes.
- **Mitochondria**: release energy (respiration).

Plant cells also have a **cell wall** (support), **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis) and a large **vacuole** (cell sap).

blocks.caption: Cell parts found in plants and in both.
blocks.alt: Six boxes: cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole in green for plants only; nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm in blue for both.

blocks.title: Levels of organisation
blocks.md:
Cells of the same kind form a **tissue** (muscle tissue). Different tissues form an **organ** (the heart). Organs that work together form an **organ system** (the circulatory system). Many systems make up an **organism**.

Some cells are specialised: a **red blood cell** carries oxygen; a **root hair cell** absorbs water; a **nerve cell** carries messages.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Animal cells do not have a cell wall or chloroplasts.
- The cell wall is not the same as the cell membrane.
- A tissue is a group of *similar cells*; an organ contains *several tissues*.

blocks.title: Plant or animal?
blocks.statement: A cell has a nucleus, a cell wall and chloroplasts. What kind of cell is it, and what is the job of the chloroplasts?
steps: A cell wall and chloroplasts are found only in plant cells.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
blocks.answer: A plant cell; chloroplasts make food by photosynthesis.

blocks.title: Order the levels
blocks.statement: Arrange: organ, cell, organism, tissue, system.
steps: Smallest to largest: cell, then tissue, then organ.
Then system and finally the whole organism.
